messages.author: b940bb03851c507a
messages.subject: userGWAS for 2-factor model
parts:
I am posting the questions and corresponding answers from Andrew Grotzinger.

Can I only get SNPs that are associated with F1 and F2 separately? Is there a way to get SNPs that can be interpreted in a way that they are associated with the model itself?

Since F1 and F2 are being modeled separately I would say that a SNP that is only associated with F1, but not F2, still fits the model. If the data told us that F1 and F2 could be merged together into a single factor then we would model it as such, and expect some SNPs to operate through that more general factor. If you are interested in SNPs that affect both F1 and F2 you could run a model where you constrain SNP effects on the factors to be equal using equality constraints and compare to a model in which those SNP effects are not constrained. The model chi-square difference between those two models indicates whether or not this is a SNP that can be reasonably interpreted as operating equally through both factors.

Also, if I filter out SNPs that are associated for both F1 and F2, then can I say that these SNPs are the ones that are associated with the 2-factor model?

Same answer as above: a SNP could only affect one factor and still be consistent with the model

Can I say that Genomic SEM requires at least 4 traits to make an interpretable model since 3 traits will always give a saturated model?

A saturated model is still interpretable in SEM space so 3 traits is fine. You can also run a two-trait factor model as long as you constraint the factor loadings to be equal.

messages.subject: Re: userGWAS for 2-factor model
parts: Below is the follow-up questions that I have regarding the answers to the previous questions.
• "Since F1 and F2 are being modeled separately I would say that a SNP that is only associated with F1, but not F2, still fits the model."
Is it applicable for the 2 factor model that has a trait cross loaded on both factors (just like the example in wiki 3 where hip circumference is cross-loaded on overweight and early life factors)?
• "If the data told us that F1 and F2 could be merged together into a single factor then we would model it as such, and expect some SNPs to operate through that more general factor."

I have also generated a common factor model and it also showed a good fit. (CFI= 0.971, SRMR=0.063) But the 2-factor model showed slightly better fit (CFI=0.996, SRMR=0.022). In this case, you are saying that although the 2-factor model shows better fit, I have to go with the common factor model?

I'd be happy to get some responses. Thank you very much.

Austin
